title: SecondChance
summary: A shelter analytics prototype that turns public records into earlier support.
tagline: A student research prototype that uses Austin Animal Center's public intake and outcome records to estimate, at intake, which animals may need extra support, and turns those estimates into a practical weekly workflow.
role: Designed and built the web application and the project presentation. Research and modeling were shared across the team.
team: Four-person UNC Charlotte team (DTSC 3601): Davis Higgins, Bennett Shearin, Seth Sumter, and Hunter Pace.

metrics.label: ROC AUC · adopted by day 30
metrics.context: 3,217 held-out stays, from the published model artifact.

metrics.label: ROC AUC · stay past 60 days
metrics.context: 3,079 held-out stays, from the published model artifact.

problem: Shelter teams have limited time and need to know which animals may benefit from extra attention early in a stay. Public intake and outcome records can help, but only if their limits are respected: transfers are not adoptions, open records are not a verified adoptable roster, and a ranking is not proof that acting on it changes outcomes.
contribution: SecondChance is a four-person UNC Charlotte project. The research and modeling were shared by the team. I designed and built the web application, which turns the team's work into a usable product, and I built the project presentation.
solution: The site connects a shelter overview, a support queue, browsable records, an outreach planner, and plain-language methodology pages. Every figure is defined once in a metric registry that feeds the dashboard tiles, chart notes, record pages, and glossary, and each page distinguishes observed outcomes, model estimates, and planning assumptions.
solutionPoints: Overview: open-stay counts, headline figures with a "what this means" note, trends, and model context.
Support queue: intake-time estimates beside actual waits, with URL-backed filters.
Record pages: stay timelines, recorded facts, data-quality notes, and suggested support.
Planner: builds a weekly outreach plan from available capacity, exportable as CSV or print.

architecture.summary: Public feeds are validated and paired into stays before any model sees them, and the site reads every metric from one committed model artifact.
flow: City of Austin intake + outcome feeds
Team modeling: two calibrated LightGBM classifiers

layers.label: Data
layers.text: Socrata feeds validated with Zod; rejected rows are counted, never silently dropped.

layers.label: Model
layers.text: Two LightGBM classifiers, calibrated with isotonic regression on a later validation block and tested on a still-later block.

layers.label: Product
layers.text: Next.js and TypeScript pages that read the artifact directly, with tests that replay the trainer's golden vectors.

decisions.title: Answer at intake.
decisions.text: Both estimates use only what is known when an animal arrives, and validation is time-based, so the scores reflect what a team could actually know.

decisions.title: Define each metric once.
decisions.text: A single registry holds each figure's meaning, unit, formula, window, sample, and limitation, so the same number never means two things on two pages.

decisions.title: Frame risk as a reason to help.
decisions.text: A higher long-stay estimate points to added support. The site says "potential benefit," never "animals saved."

outcomes: The live prototype makes the team's predictive work usable through defined metrics, browsable records, and a practical planning workflow. The published model artifact reports ROC AUC of 0.803 for 30-day adoption and 0.694 for stays past 60 days on held-out data, with calibration and subgroup checks reported on the site.
limits: SecondChance is a student research prototype and is not affiliated with the Austin Animal Center. It identifies animals that may need support; no one has shown that acting on the queue changes outcomes, which would require a prospective study. The model reflects one shelter in one city and would need local retraining elsewhere.
lessons: A model becomes useful when its estimates are translated into a clearly defined workflow, and a team project is stronger when every contribution stays visible.
